chapter_title: Designing an A/B Test with Students
learning_objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight statements is a testable hypothesis for a student A/B test or is not testable as written, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** hypothesis-sharpener
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** judge
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge whether each of eight statements is a testable hypothesis for a student A/B test or is not testable as written, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Test Hypothesis, A/B Test, Original Version, Improved Version (all defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each statement the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the five properties is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A hypothesis only needs to state what you hope. (2) A statement about the rubric score is a statement about students. (3) A hypothesis can claim that every student will benefit. **Instructional Rationale:** Judging a hypothesis against the five properties is an Evaluate-level action that every test design needs. Four testable and four untestable statements, each failing in a different way, teach the learner to look for the measure, the comparison, and the claim of every. **Content:** The two bins: Testable as written, and Not testable as written. The five properties, available on demand: specific, measurable, directional, sized, falsifiable. The eight statements (all made up, for the Watershed Basics pilot): | # | Statement | Correct bin | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Students will like the improved version. | Not testable as written | It has no comparison and no measure of liking. | | 2 | Grade 6 students who use the improved version will score at least 5 points higher on the 20-question post-test than students who use the original. | Testable as written | It names the students, the measure, the direction, and the size. | | 3 | The improved version is better. | Not testable as written | "Better" has no measure. | | 4 | A larger share of students will finish the improved version's quiz than the original's, measured by the count of completed quizzes. | Testable as written | The measure is a count, and the direction is stated. | | 5 | The improved version will raise the rubric score. | Not testable as written | The rubric score is set by reviewers, so the statement does not test an effect on students. | | 6 | Students who use the improved version will have a larger learning gain, post-test minus pre-test, than students who use the original. | Testable as written | Learning gain is defined, and the direction is stated. | | 7 | Every student will learn more from the improved version. | Not testable as written | A claim about every student cannot be shown. | | 8 | Students who use the improved version will spend less time on the task and score the same or higher on the post-test. | Testable as written | Time on task and post-test score are both measures, and the direction is stated. | **Provenance:** The statements are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The five properties follow the chapter section "Test Hypothesis". **Rules:** Each statement has exactly one correct bin, four per bin. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one statement and the two bins, and may open the five properties. Opening them does not change the score. 2. The learner places the statement in a bin, and the placement is committed. 3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text. 4. After statement 8 the sim shows the summary. **Feedback:** 8 statements in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can tell a testable hypothesis from a hope." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed statement. **Starting State:** The first statement in the shuffled order and the two bins. The question shown is "Can this be tested as written?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter lists five properties of a good hypothesis, shows a table of weak and strong hypotheses, and states the hypothesis for the Watershed Basics pilot.
